source.version: Journal version of record: Dirasat: Educational Sciences 53(3), 2026, article 13368; received 28/9/2025, revised 11/12/2025, accepted 2/2/2026, published 25/2/2026 (p. 1). Body text is in Arabic; title page has an English abstract.
source.title_on_document: Effectiveness of a Training Program Based on Artificial Intelligence Tools in Developing Creative Problem-Solving Skills

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplement or online appendix. All statistics are in Tables 1-7 and Figures 1-3 of the main text.

paper_design_summary: Seventy-five tenth-grade students in three intact mixed-gender classes of one school (Haifa District) were assigned by class to three groups of 25: a 20-session creative problem-solving program delivered with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot in the computer lab, the same program delivered with classroom strategies and no AI, or no program. The Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (verbal, Form A, Jordanian adaptation) were given before, after, and at a follow-up about three months later, and scored for fluency, flexibility, and originality. Assignment was random at the class level with one class per group; the paper calls the design quasi-experimental.

studies.label: Three-class school experiment (AI-tool training vs classroom training vs control), TTCT pre/post/follow-up

assignment.what_was_assigned: Three intact classes were randomly allocated to the three groups (AI-tool training, classroom training, control), one class per group. Students were not randomized individually.
assignment.quote: The classes were randomly assigned to three groups: the first experimental group (classroom-based training), the second experimental group (training using artificial intelligence tools), and a control group, with 25 students in each group.
assignment.locator: p. 1, English abstract (Methods); p. 6, sample section; p. 9, design diagram (R for each group); p. 5, limits section: random allocation was limited to the group level, without redistributing students within classes, because school rules forbid moving students between classes

arms.name: Experimental group 2: AI-tool training
arms.description: 20-session training program on the Osborn-Parnes creative problem-solving model, delivered in the computer lab with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot (3 sessions per week, 45 minutes each; opening and closing sessions 60 minutes).

arms.name: Experimental group 1: classroom training
arms.description: The same 20-session Osborn-Parnes program delivered in the classroom without AI, using brainstorming, problem-based and project-based learning, think-pair-share, flipped learning, and synectics.

arms.name: Control group
arms.description: No training program; took the TTCT at the same three time points.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. The 25-per-group counts are given at allocation (p. 6). Table 5 error degrees of freedom (72) are consistent with 75 students analyzed; the paper gives no separate analyzed count per arm.
participants.who: Tenth-grade students (41 male, 34 female) in three intact mixed-gender classes of one Arab school in Haifa District, chosen by convenience because the first author works there.
participants.country: Not named as a country; the population is Arab tenth-grade students in schools of Haifa District inside the Green Line (p. 6).
participants.quote: The sample comprised 75 students distributed across three intact mixed-gender tenth-grade classes in a single school.
participants.locator: p. 1, English abstract (Methods); p. 6, population and sample section

ai_tool.how_used: Students used the tools during training sessions in the computer lab: ChatGPT for interactive dialogue and generating many ideas (fluency), Gemini for varied ideas (flexibility), Copilot for new and unusual solutions (originality); Table 2 assigns one tool to each of sessions 2 to 19. The outcome test was taken after the training, not with the tools.

task.description: Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, verbal Form A, Jordanian adaptation by Al-Shanti (1983), six sub-tests (the sixth was dropped for low reliability), scored for fluency, flexibility, and originality. Given as pre-test (session 1), post-test (session 20), and follow-up test (4 September 2025).
task.duration: Program: 20 sessions, 3 per week, 45 minutes each (60 for opening and closing), 4 May to 12 June 2025 (p. 7, p. 10). Test duration not stated.

outcomes.name: TTCT fluency, post-test
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: TTCT verbal fluency score, scored according to the test instructions. Scoring reliability: two educational-psychology specialists re-scored the pilot sample; Holsti agreement 0.75 for fluency (Table 1, p. 6). Who scored the main sample is not stated. The paper does not state in so many words that AI was unavailable during the test; the post-test was given in the closing session (session 20), for which Table 2 lists no AI tool.
outcomes.delay: Post-test at the final program session (session 20); the program ended 12 June 2025.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is unclear: the paper says the three intact classes were randomly allocated to groups, but there is one class per arm and students were not randomized, so treatment is fully confounded with class (p. 5 limits section, p. 6); the paper calls its design quasi-experimental (pp. 4, 6, 9). If class-level allocation of one class per arm counts as non-random assignment of people, the study is quasi_people and belongs in observational context. Criterion 2: 75 students across arms (25 per arm). Criterion 3: TTCT fluency, flexibility, and originality scored on students' test responses, taken after the training (after_ai).

one_line_finding: In one school, the class trained with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot scored higher on the TTCT post-test than the classroom-training and control classes (originality 29.32 vs 19.48 vs 8.51; fluency 41.32 vs 33.56 vs 21.68), and the gains held at the September follow-up (Table 4, pp. 10-11).
open_questions: Does random allocation of three intact classes (one per arm) satisfy criterion 1, or is it quasi_people / observational context?
The paper does not state explicitly that AI was unavailable during the TTCT post-test; it was given in the closing session, which lists no AI tool (Table 2, p. 9).
Who scored the TTCT for the main sample, and whether scorers were blind to group, is not stated; only inter-scorer reliability on a pilot sample is reported.

No pairwise between-group comparison of post-test or follow-up scores is printed; Tables 6 and 7 report only within-group pre/post/follow-up Bonferroni differences, and the claim that the AI group outperformed the others rests on Table 4 means and the omnibus Table 5 effects.
notes: The body is in Arabic; the markdown conversion scrambles the Arabic text, so all numbers were read from the PDF page images. The AI arm differs from the classroom arm in two ways at once: AI tools and the computer-lab setting. Table 5 lists df = 1 for the within-subjects test effect despite three time points (Huynh-Feldt correction is mentioned on p. 10). Table 7 is titled as comparisons by group but repeats the within-group time comparisons of Table 6. The Table 7 entry for the AI group's fluency pre vs follow-up is printed as '*-14.70*'. TTCT scores are not standardized; no standardized between-group effect is printed besides omnibus partial eta squared.
